title: Practice Exam 2 — People, Places and Food Security
description: Application-focused paper with biome, agriculture, urban density, population-pyramid and migration stimuli.

biome.title: Stimulus C — Global biome belts
biome.text: This simplified diagram represents broad patterns in biome distribution. Use it alongside your knowledge of latitude, ocean currents, air movement, altitude, relief and distance from the sea.

image.alt: Diagram showing broad biome belts by latitude: tropical rainforest near the equator, temperate forests and grasslands in mid-latitudes, and tundra near polar latitudes, with dry subtropical belts indicated.
image.caption: Simplified conceptual diagram based on the class module; not a detailed biome map.

crop.title: Stimulus I — Crop yield and water availability
crop.text: This constructed comparison holds crop type and soil constant while changing water availability. Use it to explain one factor affecting agricultural yield.

image.alt: Bar chart showing crop yield of 1.8 tonnes per hectare with very low water, 3.6 with moderate water and 4.8 with high water availability.
image.caption: Synthetic controlled comparison; not measured farm yields.

food.title: Stimulus D — Food access index
food.text: The chart uses an invented classroom dataset to practise describing global patterns. A higher score means more reliable access to adequate food. Regions are anonymised and are not real country scores.

image.alt: Bar chart of food access scores: Region A 38, Region B 49, Region C 63, Region D 78 and Region E 86. Higher scores represent more reliable food access.
image.caption: Synthetic practice data only; not actual national or regional statistics.

landuse.title: Stimulus H — Urban land-use cross-section
landuse.text: The diagram illustrates a simplified urban pattern in which the central business district has taller and denser buildings than areas towards the edge.

image.alt: Schematic cross-section of a city with taller and denser buildings in the central business district and shorter buildings towards the urban edge.
image.caption: Illustrative diagram; not a photograph or measured city plan.

density.title: Stimulus J — Population density by area
density.text: Use the values to compare population density. Population density is the number of people per unit of land area.

image.alt: Bar chart showing Area A 850 people per square kilometre, Area B 4200, Area C 12500 and Area D 2300.
image.caption: Synthetic anonymised practice data.

pyramids.title: Stimulus F — Two population pyramids
pyramids.text: The pyramids use invented age-structure data. Compare the width of the base, working-age bands and older age groups.

image.alt: Two population pyramids with age groups from 0–14 to 75+. Population A has a wider base and narrows sharply with age. Population B has a narrower base and proportionally larger middle and older groups.
image.caption: Synthetic data; not actual country population pyramids.

migration.title: Stimulus G — International migration pathways
migration.text: This is a schematic diagram of push and pull factors and two broad forms of movement. It is not a map of a specific route or country.

image.alt: Schematic showing an origin country and a destination country connected by arrows labelled voluntary movement and forced displacement. Push factors include limited jobs, conflict and insecurity; pull factors include employment, safety and services.
image.caption: Conceptual diagram for practice; not a mapped migration route.

questions.stem: According to Stimulus C, tropical rainforest biomes are commonly found near which latitude zone?
options: The equator
The polar circles
Only 60° north
Only 60° south
questions.explanation: The diagram places tropical rainforest near the equator.

questions.stem: Which physical process helps explain why a cold ocean current can contribute to dry coastal conditions?
options: It cools air and can reduce evaporation
It always increases humidity and rainfall
It increases the height of nearby mountains
It stops the movement of all winds
questions.explanation: Cold currents cool air above the sea and can reduce evaporation, contributing to dry conditions.

questions.stem: According to Stimulus I, which water condition is associated with the greatest crop yield?
options: Very low
Moderate
High
All three are equal
questions.explanation: The high-water bar shows the greatest yield, 4.8 tonnes per hectare.

questions.stem: What does the food access score in Stimulus D represent?
options: The number of crops grown
A practice measure of reliability of access to adequate food
The area of farmland in each region
The percentage of people living in cities
questions.explanation: The stimulus states that higher scores represent more reliable access to adequate food.

questions.stem: What feature of Stimulus H indicates a higher-density central business district?
options: Taller and more closely grouped buildings
Fewer buildings and larger open blocks
A greater distance between buildings
A predominance of farmland
questions.explanation: The diagram shows taller, more closely grouped buildings in the central area.

questions.stem: Which area has the greatest population density in Stimulus J?
options: Area A
Area B
Area C
Area D
questions.explanation: Area C has 12,500 people per square kilometre, the largest value.

questions.stem: Which statement best compares Population A and Population B in Stimulus F?
options: A has a wider base; B has relatively larger middle and older groups
A has no children; B has no older people
Both have exactly the same age structure
B has a wider base and a much smaller older population
questions.explanation: Population A has the wider base, while Population B has proportionally larger middle and older age groups.

questions.stem: A person who has applied for protection in another country and is waiting for a decision is generally described as:
options: An asylum seeker
A tourist
A seasonal holiday-maker
A returning resident
questions.explanation: An asylum seeker has requested protection and is awaiting a decision on the claim.

questions.stem: What is the broad purpose of a skilled migration points-based approach?
options: To select applicants against a set of relevant criteria
To guarantee permanent residence to every applicant
To prevent all movement between countries
To assess only the applicant’s preferred city
questions.explanation: A points-based approach is used to assess applicants against relevant selection criteria; it does not guarantee a visa.

questions.stem: If a country receives a substantial inflow of working-age migrants, which population-pyramid change may occur?
options: An increase in some working-age cohorts
The immediate removal of all older age groups
A guaranteed fall in the total population
An identical reduction in every age group
questions.explanation: Migration can increase the size of age groups represented by the people arriving.

questions.stem: Using Stimulus C and your geographical knowledge, explain how latitude and two other physical factors influence the distribution of biomes. (5 marks)
criteria: Explains how latitude changes solar angle/energy and temperature patterns.
Explains the influence of ocean currents on temperature or rainfall.
Explains the influence of mountain barriers/relief or altitude on climate.
Links the physical factors to differences in vegetation and biome distribution.
Uses a relevant biome example, such as tropical rainforest, desert, temperate grassland or tundra.
questions.model: Latitude affects the amount and intensity of solar energy received, so temperatures generally decrease towards higher latitudes. Ocean currents can warm or cool coastal air and affect rainfall. Mountain barriers can force air to rise, producing wetter conditions on one side and a rain shadow on the other, while altitude generally lowers temperature. These climate differences help determine the vegetation and biome found in an area.

questions.stem: Using Stimulus I, explain how water availability can affect agricultural yield. Then identify one other challenge to food production and explain its impact. (5 marks)
criteria: Identifies the yield difference between low and high water conditions using values.
Explains why crops need water for growth and how scarcity can reduce yields.
Identifies a second challenge such as soil degradation, salinity, pollution or competing land use.
Explains how the second challenge affects soil, water, available land or farm productivity.
Links reduced or unstable production to potential food-security effects.
questions.model: In the practice data, yield rises from 1.8 tonnes per hectare under very low water to 4.8 tonnes per hectare under high water. Crops need water for growth, so water scarcity can limit yields. Soil degradation is another challenge: erosion or salinity can reduce soil quality and make farmland less productive. Lower production can contribute to food insecurity, especially where people also have limited economic access to food.

questions.stem: Use Stimuli H and J to explain the difference between population density and urbanisation, and identify one challenge that may result from rapid urban growth. (5 marks)
criteria: Defines population density as population per unit area.
Defines urbanisation as an increase in the proportion of people living in urban areas.
Uses the density graph accurately to compare at least two areas.
Explains one urban growth challenge such as housing, transport, water or sanitation pressure.
Links planning and infrastructure provision to management of urban growth.
questions.model: Population density is the number of people per unit of land area, while urbanisation is the increasing proportion of a population living in urban areas. In Stimulus J, Area C has the highest density at 12,500 people per square kilometre, compared with Area A at 850. Rapid urban growth can create pressure on housing and transport if infrastructure does not keep pace. Effective planning can improve access to services and reduce these problems.

questions.stem: Compare the age structures shown in Stimulus F and explain how international migration could change the population structure of either population. (5 marks)
criteria: Identifies Population A as having a broad base and larger younger cohorts.
Identifies Population B as having a narrower base and relatively larger middle/older cohorts.
Explains one reason for different pyramid shapes, such as birth rates or life expectancy.
Explains how migration can add people to particular working-age or family age groups.
Links the age-structure change to a possible origin or destination-country impact.
questions.model: Population A has a broad base, suggesting a larger proportion of children, while Population B has a narrower base and larger middle and older groups. Differences may be linked to birth rates and life expectancy. If a country receives many working-age migrants, the corresponding age cohorts may increase; if people of working age leave, the origin country may have a smaller workforce in those age groups.

questions.stem: Evaluate the effects of skilled and forced international migration on Australia and on countries of origin. Refer to the role of Australia’s points-based skilled migration approach, refugees and asylum seekers, and one international example. (15 marks)
criteria: Introduces a clear judgement about whether international migration is more beneficial, challenging or mixed overall.
Defines international migration accurately as movement across an international border.
Distinguishes voluntary migration from forced migration.
Explains at least one push factor that can encourage people to leave an origin country.
Explains at least one pull factor that can attract people to a destination country.
Explains a positive impact on a host country, such as filling skill shortages or supporting economic activity.
Explains a possible challenge for a host country, such as pressure on housing or services if planning is inadequate.
Explains a positive impact on an origin country, such as remittances or diaspora links.
Explains a possible negative impact on an origin country, such as loss of skilled workers or family separation.
Explains the broad purpose of skilled migration selection in Australia.
Refers to Australia’s points-based approach without inventing a points threshold or guaranteed visa outcome.
Distinguishes a refugee from an asylum seeker accurately.
Uses Australia and at least one other international migration example relevantly.
Uses evidence or stimulus information to support the discussion rather than listing impacts only.
Finishes with a reasoned conclusion that weighs impacts on both origin and host countries.
questions.model:
International migration is the movement of people across an international border to live in another country. Its effects are mixed because it can create opportunities for migrants and destination countries, while also producing challenges for origin countries and communities. Voluntary migrants may move for employment, education or family reasons, whereas forced migrants leave because of serious threats such as conflict or persecution. A refugee is outside their country and meets the relevant protection definition; an asylum seeker has requested protection and is waiting for a decision.

In a host country such as Australia, skilled migration can help address labour shortages, contribute to economic activity and add skills and cultural knowledge. Australia's skilled migration settings include a points-based pathway, which is designed to select applicants against relevant criteria; meeting a points threshold alone should not be described as a guaranteed visa. Migration can also increase demand for housing, schools, health care and transport when population growth is not matched by planning and investment.

Origin countries may benefit when migrants send remittances to relatives, maintain business links or return with new skills. However, the departure of trained workers can contribute to a loss of skills, and migration can separate families. The Mexico–USA corridor is an international example in which employment, family links, border rules and the risks of irregular movement can all shape migration decisions. Humanitarian migration provides a different example because safety and protection, rather than simply seeking better employment, are central. Overall, migration is not automatically positive or negative: its effects depend on who moves, why they move, the rights and conditions they experience, and how well origin and host countries plan for change.
